query: For high-entropy alloys intended for demanding engineering applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs the retention or loss of toughness, and why? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Toughness retention or loss in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) under demanding conditions is primarily governed by element segregation at grain boundaries, which alters local cohesion and promotes intergranular fracture upon mechanical or thermal loading.
generation.material_initial_state: A near-homogeneous, single-phase HEA with minimal initial segregation and uniformly distributed elements at the grain boundaries.
generation.intervention: Perform in-situ, elevated-temperature fracture or crack-growth experiments in SEM/TEM, using controlled annealing and cooling (fast versus slow) to selectively vary grain boundary chemistry and monitor crack propagation in real time.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperatures (e.g., 600–1000 °C), representative of severe service environments, combined with slow strain-rate or sustained loading to facilitate potential grain boundary segregation and embrittlement phenomena.
generation.structural_mediator: Time- and temperature-dependent elemental diffusion leading to local enrichment of specific atoms at grain boundaries and increased susceptibility to intergranular cracking.
generation.mechanism: Thermally driven boundary segregation of embrittling elements diminishes cohesive strength at interfaces, thereby promoting intergranular crack nucleation and propagation, lowering toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples exposed to slower cooling or higher annealing temperatures that promote increased boundary segregation will exhibit reduced fracture energy and a shift from transgranular to intergranular cracking relative to a fast-quenched or otherwise homogenized baseline.
generation.baseline: An as-prepared, homogenized alloy with minimal grain boundary segregation, displaying comparatively higher toughness and predominantly transgranular fracture at moderate service temperatures.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to single-phase or near-single-phase HEAs under temperature and time regimes that allow sufficient diffusion for appreciable element segregation; at very low temperatures or in alloys with negligible GB diffusivity, its validity may diminish.
generation.uncertainty: Though evidence strongly implicates boundary segregation, other factors (e.g., short-range order, nanoscale precipitation, dislocation substructures) could also modulate toughness loss, requiring further careful distinction between these effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Analyze two sets of HEA specimens in side-by-side in-situ elevated-temperature SEM/TEM tensile tests: one set with intentionally enhanced boundary segregation (via slow cooling or specific alloy modification) and another with minimal segregation (fast quenching). Observe crack formation and progression in real time under the same mechanical loading conditions.
measurements: Local grain boundary chemistry using EDS or atom-probe tomography
Quantification of fracture surfaces (intergranular versus transgranular) via SEM images
In-situ observation of microstructural changes (e.g., boundary phases, dislocations)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If specimens with heightened grain boundary segregation do not exhibit significantly reduced toughness or intergranular cracking behavior—and if those with minimal boundary segregation show similar embrittlement—then the proposed mechanism of segregation-driven intergranular fracture would be refuted.

cited_evidence.text: During the tensile test process at intermediate temperatures in the air, intermetallic phases were not yet formed in coarse-grained Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni HEAs, owing to a short testing time (a few minutes). In addition, the above-mentioned oxide and hydrogen embrittlement mechanisms can be ruled out because these alloys show good resistance to oxidation at intermediate temperatures and hydrogen embrittlement at relatively low hydrogen concentrations (, ). These facts suggest that temperature-induced ductility loss in fcc-phase HEAs/MEAs could be related to segregation of some of the principal elements during the short testing time, which causes GB decohesion. We examined this hypothesis in an equiatomic Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEA and revealed the fast segregation of Cr, Mn, and Ni separately into GBs, which accounts for ductility loss with increasing temperature. Correspondingly, we proposed and demonstrated that preexisting precipitates can migrate the fast segregation of Cr, Mn, and Ni into the precipitates instead of at GBs, which can effectively evade ductility loss during deformation at intermediate temperatures.

ABSTRACTIn this study, tensile and creep deformation of a high-entropy alloy processed by selective laser melting (SLM) has been investigated; hot ductility drop was identified at first, and the loss of ductility at elevated temperature was associated with intergranular fracture. By modifying the grain boundary morphology from straight to serration, the hot ductility drop issue has been resolved successfully. The serrated grain boundary could be achieved by reducing the cooling rate of solution heat treatment, which allowed the coarsening of L12 structured γ′ precipitates to interfere with mobile grain boundaries, resulting in undulation of the grain boundary morphology. Tensile and creep tests at 650°C were conducted, and serrated grain boundary could render a significant increase in tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life by a factor of 3.5 and 400, respectively. Detailed microstructure analysis has indicated that serrated grain boundary could distribute strains more evenly than that of straight morphology. The effect of serrated grain boundary on tensile and creep properties has been investigated for a high-entropy alloy (Al8Co35Cr18Ni34Ti3Nb2Zr0.005B0.01 (at.%)) fabricated by selective laser melting, the followings are findings of this work: Serrated grain boundary could render a significant increase in tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life by a factor of 3.5 and 400, respectively. The inferior ductility of straight grain boundary at 650°C was attributed to the grain boundary embrittlement caused by strain concentration at triple junctions and fast intergranular crack propagation. The slow cooling process of the post heat treatment could coarsen the γ′ particles and encourage interactions with mobile grain boundaries to from serrated grain boundaries. Analysis has indicated that serrated grain boundary could distribute strains more evenly than that of straight morphology. Serrated grain boundaries could reduce local strain concentration and provide resistance against intergranular cracking.

decision.trend: Early work (PMC6006257) demonstrated that unexpected twinning in metastable high-entropy alloys can boost both strength and ductility, but left open how these mechanisms scale under demanding conditions or long-term loading. Later (PMC6897545) it was discovered that grain boundary nanoclustering of certain principal elements promoted grain boundary cracking and ductility (thus toughness) loss, revealing that local segregation at boundaries is a central driver. Although grain boundary engineering was proposed as a partial fix, the precise mechanistic pathway controlling the retention or degradation of toughness in diverse stress and temperature regimes remains an open challenge.
decision.unsolved: It is still unclear how to isolate the distinct roles of local phase or order transitions versus boundary segregation in controlling fracture resistance under real engineering conditions. Determining which microstructural changes — e.g., short-range ordering, grain boundary chemical composition, or dislocation substructure — most strongly determine the onset of toughness loss requires targeted validation.
decision.lever: Perform in-situ, elevated-temperature fracture or crack-growth experiments in a scanning/transmission electron microscope with site-specific control of boundary character and annealing treatment (cooling rates, annealing temperature/time), while tracking grain boundary segregation and evolving dislocation structures in real-time.
decision.why: Because prior work implicates local compositional and structural shifts in controlling ductility or embrittlement, dynamic in-situ tracking of these microstructural evolutions during deformation will reveal which factors most directly govern the retention or loss of toughness under demanding conditions, thereby testing whether grain-boundary or phase-related transformations dominate.
